subject: maths
title: Year 6 Transformations and Tessellations
seo_title: Year 6 Transformations and Tessellations Worksheets: Free Maths with Answer Key (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: recognise and use combinations of transformations to create tessellations and other geometric patterns, using dynamic geometric software where appropriate
meta_desc: Free Year 6 maths worksheets on transformations and tessellations, aligned to the Australian Curriculum (AC9M6SP03): translations, reflections and rotations, combinations of moves, which shapes tessellate and why (angles at a point), tile patterns and design problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: A shape tessellates when copies fit around every point with no gaps or overlaps: the angles there must add up to 360°.
key_sub: Translate = slide, reflect = flip, rotate = turn. Equilateral triangles (6 × 60°), squares (4 × 90°) and regular hexagons (3 × 120°) tessellate; regular pentagons, octagons and circles do not.
body_html:
Three ways to move a shape

A translation slides a shape. A reflection flips it in a mirror line, so it becomes a mirror image. A rotation turns it about a point. The shape stays the same size and keeps the same angles.

MoveFaces the same way?Check
translation (slide)yesevery corner moves the same distance in the same direction
reflection (flip)no: mirror imageeach corner is the same distance from the mirror line, on the other side
rotation (turn)turnedone point (the centre) stays still

Combinations of transformations

You can do one move after another. Do the steps in order, and follow one corner through each step.

Example 1

Reflect (2, 3) in the line x = 5, then translate it 2 squares up.

(2, 3) is 3 squares left of x = 5, so its image is 3 squares right: (8, 3). Then 2 up: (8, 5).

Answer: (8, 5)

A reflection followed by a translation along the mirror line is like a trail of footprints: left, right, left, right.

Tessellations

A shape tessellates when copies of it cover a surface with no gaps and no overlaps. Where the corners meet, the angles must add up to 360°.

Regular shapeEach angleAround a pointTessellates on its own?
equilateral triangle60°6 × 60° = 360°yes
square90°4 × 90° = 360°yes
regular hexagon120°3 × 120° = 360°yes
regular pentagon108°3 × 108° = 324° (gap)no
regular octagon135°2 × 135° = 270° (gap)no

Circles never tessellate: curved edges leave gaps. Any triangle and any quadrilateral tessellates, because their angles can fill 360°.

Example 2

Two regular hexagons meet at a point. How many equilateral triangles fill the gap?

2 × 120° = 240°. 360° − 240° = 120°. 120° ÷ 60° = 2.

Answer: 2 triangles

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Calling a half turn a reflection because the shape is upside downCheck for a mirror image: a half turn also swaps left and right
Thinking all regular shapes tessellateOnly triangles, squares and hexagons: their angles divide exactly into 360°
Doing a combination in the wrong orderDo the steps in the order given and follow one corner
Measuring the translation straight from the first shape to the lastDo the reflection first, then measure the slide

faq.q: What do Year 6 students learn about transformations and tessellations in the Australian Curriculum?
faq.a: In Year 6 (AC9M6SP03) students recognise and use combinations of translations, reflections and rotations to create tessellations and other geometric patterns, often using geometry software.
Equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons tessellate on their own, and so does any triangle or quadrilateral. Regular pentagons, regular octagons and circles do not.

faq.q: Why does a regular pentagon not tessellate?
faq.a: Each angle is 108°. Three pentagons make 324°, leaving a 36° gap, and four make 432°, which overlaps, so they cannot fill the 360° around a point.

faq.q: What is a combination of transformations?
faq.a: It is two or more moves done one after another, such as a reflection followed by a translation. Do the steps in order; changing the order can give a different result.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: Every corner of B is the same number of squares from its matching corner of A, in the same direction, and B faces the same way. It was slid: a translation. Every corner moved 5 squares right and 4 squares up.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: Every corner of B is the same number of squares from its matching corner of A, in the same direction, and B faces the same way. It was slid: a translation. Every corner moved 5 squares right and 4 squares down.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is a mirror image of A: it faces the other way. Each corner of B is the same distance from the mirror line as its partner in A. It was flipped: a reflection. The mirror line is x = 5.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is a mirror image of A: it faces the other way. Each corner of B is the same distance from the mirror line as its partner in A. It was flipped: a reflection. The mirror line is y = 4: B is upside down but is not turned.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is a mirror image of A: it faces the other way. Each corner of B is the same distance from the mirror line as its partner in A. It was flipped: a reflection. The slanted side is on the left of A and on the right of B, at the same height.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. Point O does not move. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is A turned about the point O: it is not flipped (it is not a mirror image), and O does not move. It is a rotation. The side that pointed right from O now points down: a quarter turn clockwise.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. Point O does not move. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is A turned about the point O: it is not flipped (it is not a mirror image), and O does not move. It is a rotation. It is a half turn about O. It looks upside down, but a reflection in a horizontal line would not also swap left and right.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. Point O does not move. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is A turned about the point O: it is not flipped (it is not a mirror image), and O does not move. It is a rotation. The bottom side pointed right from O and now points up: a quarter turn anticlockwise.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: The sides of B are twice as long as the sides of A. A translation, reflection or rotation never changes the size, so B was enlarged. The bottom side of A is 3 squares long; the bottom side of B is 6 squares long.

items.q: In which picture is the blue shape a reflection of the green shape?
items.e: In C the blue shape is reflected in a vertical line: it faces the other way, left to right. The others: A is turned a quarter turn clockwise; B is slid (a translation): it faces the same way; D is turned a half turn: upside down and back to front.

items.q: In which picture is the blue shape a translation of the green shape?
items.e: In A the blue shape is slid (a translation): it faces the same way. The others: B is turned a quarter turn anticlockwise; C is turned a half turn: upside down and back to front; D is reflected in a horizontal line: it is flipped upside down only.

items.q: In which picture is the blue shape a rotation of the green shape?
items.e: In D the blue shape is turned a quarter turn clockwise. The others: A is reflected in a vertical line: it faces the other way, left to right; B is slid (a translation): it faces the same way; C is reflected in a horizontal line: it is flipped upside down only.

items.q: In which picture is the blue shape the green shape reflected in a horizontal mirror line?
items.e: In B the blue shape is reflected in a horizontal line: it is flipped upside down only. The others: A is slid (a translation): it faces the same way; C is reflected in a vertical line: it faces the other way, left to right; D is turned a half turn: upside down and back to front.

items.q: The letter b is reflected in a vertical mirror line (flipped left to right). Which letter does it look like?
items.e: A vertical mirror flips left and right, so the round part moves to the other side of the stick but stays at the bottom: d.

items.q: The letter b is reflected in a horizontal mirror line (flipped upside down). Which letter does it look like?
items.e: A horizontal mirror flips top and bottom, so the stick now hangs down and the round part stays on the right: p.

items.q: The letter b is rotated a half turn. Which letter does it look like?
items.e: A half turn turns it upside down and back to front at the same time: the stick hangs down and the round part is on the left: q. This is not the same as a reflection.

items.q: A lift goes straight up from the ground floor to level 3. Which transformation is this?
items.e: The lift slides in one direction without turning or flipping, so it is a translation.

items.q: A door swings open on its hinges. Which transformation is this?
items.e: The door turns about a fixed line (the hinges). Seen from above, it turns about a point: a rotation.

items.q: Shape B is shape A turned a half turn. Amelia says, “B is upside down, so it must be a reflection.” What is wrong?
c: A reflection never turns a shape upside down
Nothing: upside down always means a reflection
A half turn makes the shape smaller
A half turn also turns a shape upside down
items.e: A half turn turns a shape upside down and back to front. A reflection makes a mirror image. Check: is B a mirror image of A, or is it A turned?

items.q: After a translation, a reflection or a rotation, which of these always stays the same?
items.e: These moves change where the shape is (and a reflection or rotation changes the way it faces), but never its size. The side lengths and angles always stay the same.

items.q: Point (2, 3) is reflected in the vertical mirror line x = 5, then translated 2 squares up. Where does it end up?
items.e: Do the steps in order. Step 1: The point (2, 3) is 3 squares to the left of the line x = 5. The image is 3 squares to the right of it: 5 + 3 = 8. y stays 3. The image is (8, 3). Step 2: (8, 3) → (8, 5). x stays 8. Up 2 squares changes y: 3 + 2 = 5. The new point is (8, 5).

items.q: Point (7, 1) is reflected in the horizontal mirror line y = 3, then translated 4 squares left. Where does it end up?
items.e: Do the steps in order. Step 1: The point (7, 1) is 2 squares below the line y = 3. The image is 2 squares above it: 3 + 2 = 5. x stays 7. The image is (7, 5). Step 2: (7, 5) → (3, 5). Left 4 squares changes x: 7 − 4 = 3. y stays 5. The new point is (3, 5).

items.q: Point (1, 6) is reflected in the vertical mirror line x = 4, then translated 3 squares down. Where does it end up?
items.e: Do the steps in order. Step 1: The point (1, 6) is 3 squares to the left of the line x = 4. The image is 3 squares to the right of it: 4 + 3 = 7. y stays 6. The image is (7, 6). Step 2: (7, 6) → (7, 3). x stays 7. Down 3 squares changes y: 6 − 3 = 3. The new point is (7, 3).

items.q: Point (6, 8) is reflected in the horizontal mirror line y = 6, then translated 2 squares right. Where does it end up?
items.e: Do the steps in order. Step 1: The point (6, 8) is 2 squares above the line y = 6. The image is 2 squares below it: 6 − 2 = 4. x stays 6. The image is (6, 4). Step 2: (6, 4) → (8, 4). Right 2 squares changes x: 6 + 2 = 8. y stays 4. The new point is (8, 4).

items.q: Point (3, 2) is translated 2 squares right, then reflected in the vertical mirror line x = 6. Where does it end up?
items.e: Do the steps in order. Step 1: (3, 2) → (5, 2). Right 2 squares changes x: 3 + 2 = 5. y stays 2. The new point is (5, 2). Step 2: The point (5, 2) is 1 square to the left of the line x = 6. The image is 1 square to the right of it: 6 + 1 = 7. y stays 2. The image is (7, 2).

items.q: Point (2, 7) is translated 2 squares down, then reflected in the horizontal mirror line y = 4. Where does it end up?
items.e: Do the steps in order. Step 1: (2, 7) → (2, 5). x stays 2. Down 2 squares changes y: 7 − 2 = 5. The new point is (2, 5). Step 2: The point (2, 5) is 1 square above the line y = 4. The image is 1 square below it: 4 − 1 = 3. x stays 2. The image is (2, 3).

items.q: Point (7, 4) is rotated a quarter turn clockwise about (5, 4), then translated 3 squares right. Where does it end up?
items.e: Do the steps in order. Step 1: From the centre (5, 4), the point (7, 4) is 2 right. In a quarter turn clockwise, right turns into down, down into left, left into up and up into right. So the image is 2 down from the centre: (5, 2). Step 2: (5, 2) → (8, 2). Right 3 squares changes x: 5 + 3 = 8. y stays 2. The new point is (8, 2).

items.q: Point (5, 6) is rotated a half turn about (5, 4), then translated 2 squares left. Where does it end up?
items.e: Do the steps in order. Step 1: From the centre (5, 4), the point (5, 6) is 2 up. In a half turn, right turns into left and up turns into down. So the image is 2 down from the centre: (5, 2). Step 2: (5, 2) → (3, 2). Left 2 squares changes x: 5 − 2 = 3. y stays 2. The new point is (3, 2).

items.q: Point (8, 2) is rotated a quarter turn anticlockwise about (6, 2), then translated 3 squares up. Where does it end up?
items.e: Do the steps in order. Step 1: From the centre (6, 2), the point (8, 2) is 2 right. In a quarter turn anticlockwise, right turns into up, up into left, left into down and down into right. So the image is 2 up from the centre: (6, 4). Step 2: (6, 4) → (6, 7). x stays 6. Up 3 squares changes y: 4 + 3 = 7. The new point is (6, 7).

items.q: A shape is translated 3 squares right and 2 squares up, then 4 squares right and 5 squares down. Which single translation does the same?
items.e: Combine the moves across and the moves up and down. Across: 3 right and 4 right make 7 right. Up and down: 2 up and 5 down make 3 down. So the single translation is 7 squares right and 3 squares down.

items.q: A shape is translated 5 squares left and 1 square up, then 2 squares right and 4 squares up. Which single translation does the same?
items.e: Combine the moves across and the moves up and down. Across: 5 left and 2 right make 3 left. Up and down: 1 up and 4 up make 5 up. So the single translation is 3 squares left and 5 squares up.

items.q: Shape A is reflected in the dashed mirror line. Then the image is translated to make shape C. Describe the translation.
items.e: First reflect A in x = 5: the corner (1, 5) goes to (9, 5). Then follow that corner to C: (9, 5) → (9, 1) is 4 squares down. Do not measure straight from A to C (that gives 8 right, 4 down): A has to be reflected first.

items.q: Shape A is reflected in the dashed mirror line. Then the image is translated to make shape C. Describe the translation.
items.e: First reflect A in y = 4: the corner (1, 1) goes to (1, 7). Then follow that corner to C: (1, 7) → (6, 7) is 5 squares right. Do not measure straight from A to C (that gives 5 right, 6 up): A has to be reflected first.

items.q: Shape A is reflected in the dashed mirror line. Then the image is translated to make shape C. Describe the translation.
items.e: First reflect A in x = 5: the corner (1, 1) goes to (9, 1). Then follow that corner to C: (9, 1) → (9, 6) is 5 squares up. Do not measure straight from A to C (that gives 8 right, 5 up): A has to be reflected first.

items.q: Which two steps move shape A onto shape C?
c: reflect in x = 5, then translate 3 up
reflect in y = 5, then translate 3 right
items.e: C is a mirror image of A, so one step must be a reflection. Check it corner by corner: (1, 2) → (9, 5), (4, 2) → (6, 5), so it gives C. The others do not: “translate 5 right, then translate 3 up” puts A at (6, 5), (9, 5), …; “reflect in y = 5, then translate 3 right” puts A at (4, 8), (7, 8), …; “rotate a half turn about (5, 4)” puts A at (9, 6), (6, 6), ….

items.q: Which two steps move shape A onto shape C?
c: reflect in y = 4, then translate 5 right
reflect in x = 5, then translate 4 down
items.e: C is a mirror image of A, so one step must be a reflection. Check it corner by corner: (1, 5) → (6, 3), (4, 5) → (9, 3), so it gives C. The others do not: “translate 5 right, then translate 4 down” puts A at (6, 1), (9, 1), …; “rotate a half turn about (5, 4)” puts A at (9, 3), (6, 3), …; “reflect in x = 5, then translate 4 down” puts A at (9, 1), (6, 1), ….

items.q: A shape is reflected in the line x = 5, then the image is reflected in the line y = 4. Which single move does the same?
c: a reflection in the line y = 4
items.e: Two reflections in lines that cross at right angles make a half turn about the point where they cross, (5, 4). For example (2, 1) → (8, 1) → (8, 7), and a half turn about (5, 4) also takes (2, 1) to (8, 7).

items.q: A shape is reflected in the line x = 2, then the image is reflected in the line x = 5. Which single move does the same?
c: a reflection in the line x = 7
items.e: Two reflections in parallel lines make a translation of twice the gap between the lines: 2 × 3 = 6 squares right. For example (3, 1) → (1, 1) → (9, 1), which is 6 squares right of (3, 1).

items.q: Point (2, 3) is reflected in x = 4 and translated 3 squares right. Does the order of the two steps matter?
c: Yes, but only the y-coordinate changes
items.e: Reflect first: (2, 3) → (6, 3) → (9, 3). Translate first: (2, 3) → (5, 3) → (3, 3). The answers are different, so do the steps in the order given.

items.q: A shape is rotated a quarter turn clockwise about a point, then another quarter turn clockwise about the same point. Which single move does the same?
c: a half turn about that point
items.e: Two quarter turns make a half turn: 90° + 90° = 180°.

sets.title: Which shapes tessellate? Angles at a point

items.q: Each angle of a square is 90°. How many squares fit together around one point with no gaps?
items.e: The angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° ÷ 90° = 4, so 4 squares fit exactly around each point.

items.q: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°. How many equilateral triangles fit together around one point with no gaps?
items.e: The angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° ÷ 60° = 6, so 6 equilateral triangles fit exactly around each point.

items.q: Each angle of a regular hexagon is 120°. How many regular hexagons fit together around one point with no gaps?
items.e: The angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° ÷ 120° = 3, so 3 regular hexagons fit exactly around each point.

items.q: Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°. Can regular pentagons fit around a point with no gaps?
items.e: 3 × 108° = 324°, which is less than 360°, so there is a gap of 36°. 4 × 108° = 432°, which is more than 360°, so a fourth pentagon would overlap. Regular pentagons do not tessellate.

items.q: Three regular pentagons meet at the red dot. Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°. What is the size of the gap?
items.e: 3 × 108° = 324°. A full turn is 360°, so the gap is 360° − 324° = 36°. No regular shape has a 36° angle, so the gap cannot be filled with the same tiles.

items.q: Each angle of a regular octagon is 135°. Why do regular octagons not tessellate on their own?
items.e: Around a point the angles must add up to exactly 360°. 2 × 135° = 270° leaves a gap and 3 × 135° = 405° is too much. 135° does not divide exactly into 360°.

items.q: What does it mean when a shape tessellates?
c: Copies of it fit together with small gaps between them
It has at least one line of symmetry
It can be turned onto itself
Copies of it fit together with no gaps and no overlaps
items.e: A tessellation is a pattern of shapes that covers a surface with no gaps and no overlaps, like the tiles on a floor.

items.q: Which shape tessellates on its own?
items.e: The regular hexagon (D): each angle is 120° and 3 × 120° = 360°. A regular pentagon (108°) and a regular octagon (135°) leave gaps, and circles cannot fit together without gaps.

items.q: Which shape does NOT tessellate on its own?
items.e: The regular pentagon (A): its angles are 108° and 360° ÷ 108° is not a whole number. Squares (4 × 90°), equilateral triangles (6 × 60°) and regular hexagons (3 × 120°) all fit exactly around a point.

items.q: Why do circles not tessellate?
c: They have no angles, so they fit anywhere
Their curved edges always leave gaps
items.e: When circles touch, there are always curved gaps between them. A tessellation can have no gaps.

items.q: Which regular shapes tessellate on their own?
c: Every regular shape with an even number of sides
Only equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons
items.e: A regular shape tessellates only if its angle divides exactly into 360°: 60° (6 fit), 90° (4 fit) and 120° (3 fit). Regular pentagons (108°) and octagons (135°) do not, even though octagons have an even number of sides.

items.q: Mei says, “All regular shapes tessellate.” Which shape shows that she is wrong?
items.e: Regular pentagons leave a 36° gap around a point (3 × 108° = 324°). Squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons do tessellate, so they do not show Mei is wrong.

items.q: In a tessellation, what do the angles that meet at a point add up to?
items.e: The shapes go all the way around the point with no gaps and no overlaps: a full turn, 360°. (180° is the angles on a straight line or in a triangle.)

items.q: A regular shape tessellates on its own only if its angle divides exactly into 360°. Which angle works?
items.e: 360° ÷ 120° = 3 exactly. 360 ÷ 108, 360 ÷ 135 and 360 ÷ 140 are not whole numbers, so those shapes leave gaps.

items.q: Do rectangles tessellate?
c: Yes: four 90° corners fill the 360° around a point
Only if they are turned on an angle
No: their sides are not all equal
items.e: Each corner of a rectangle is 90°, and 4 × 90° = 360°. Rows of rectangles, like bricks or floorboards, cover a surface with no gaps. The sides do not need to be equal.

items.q: Copies of any triangle can tessellate. A triangle has angles of 50°, 60° and 70°. In a tessellation of this triangle, each angle appears twice at every meeting point. How many triangles meet at each point?
items.e: Each angle appears twice: 2 × (50° + 60° + 70°) = 2 × 180° = 360°. That is 6 angles, so 6 triangles meet at each point.

items.q: Two regular octagons meet at the red dot. Each angle of a regular octagon is 135°. What is the size of the gap?
items.e: 2 × 135° = 270°, and 360° − 270° = 90°. A square fits the gap exactly, so octagons and squares tessellate together.

items.q: Two regular hexagons meet at the red dot. How many equilateral triangles fill the gap?
items.e: 2 × 120° = 240°, so the gap is 360° − 240° = 120°. Each equilateral triangle has 60° angles: 120° ÷ 60° = 2 triangles.

items.q: Two squares meet at a point. How many equilateral triangles fill the rest of the space around the point?
items.e: 2 × 90° = 180°, so 360° − 180° = 180° is left. 180° ÷ 60° = 3 equilateral triangles.

items.q: Each angle of a regular dodecagon (12 sides) is 150°. Does it tessellate on its own?
c: Yes: it has an even number of sides
items.e: 2 × 150° = 300° leaves a 60° gap and 3 × 150° = 450° overlaps. 360° ÷ 150° is not a whole number, so it does not tessellate on its own. (The 60° gap could be filled by an equilateral triangle.)

sets.title: Tessellating patterns in tiles and art

items.q: In this brick wall, how is each row placed compared with the row below it?
items.e: Each row is the row below slid half a brick sideways (and up one row). Nothing is flipped or turned, so it is a translation.

items.q: How many hexagons meet at the red dot?
items.e: 3 hexagons meet at each corner. Each angle is 120°, and 3 × 120° = 360°.

items.q: How many triangles meet at the red dot?
items.e: 6 triangles meet at each point. Each angle is 60°, and 6 × 60° = 360°.

items.q: Which two shapes make this floor tile pattern?
items.e: The large tiles have 8 equal sides (regular octagons) and the small tiles are squares turned on an angle. At each corner, 135° + 135° + 90° = 360°.

items.q: How many tiles meet at the red dot?
items.e: 2 octagons and 1 square meet at each corner: 135° + 135° + 90° = 360°.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: Every flag points the same way and is the same way up. Each one is the one before slid 1 tile to the right.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: The flags point right, left, right, left but stay the same way up: each is a mirror image of the one before, with the mirror line on the edge between the tiles. A half turn would also turn it upside down.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: Each flag is upside down and points the other way. It is the one before turned a half turn about the middle of the edge between the tiles. A reflection flips it only one way.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: Each flag is upside down but still points right. It is reflected in the line across the middle of the strip and then slid 1 tile along, like a trail of footprints.

items.q: Each tile is the tile before turned a quarter turn clockwise. Which tile comes next?
items.e: The flag on the pole points right, then down, then left. One more quarter turn clockwise makes it point up: B. The others: A: it is turned anticlockwise, back to the second tile; C: it is turned one quarter turn too far, back to the start; D: it is a mirror image of the right answer, flipped, not turned.

items.q: Which pattern is a tessellation?
items.e: A tessellation has no gaps and no overlaps. Only the squares (C) fit together with no gaps. The others: A: the circles leave curved gaps; B: the octagons leave square gaps; D: the pentagons leave a gap.

items.q: This quilt block has 4 small squares. How is each small square made from the one before it, going round clockwise?
c: a reflection in the line between them
a half turn about the centre of the block
a quarter turn clockwise about the centre of the block
items.e: Look at the side of each red triangle that runs the whole width of its small square: it lies along the top of the block, then the right side, then the bottom, then the left. Each square is the one before turned 90° clockwise about the centre. A reflection would make a mirror image.

items.q: An artist cuts a bump out of the left side of a square tile and sticks the same bump on the right side, without turning it. Will copies of the new tile still tessellate?
c: No: curved edges always leave gaps
Only if the bump is cut off again
Yes: each bump fits into the gap in the next tile
items.e: The bump was translated from one side to the opposite side, so the shape of the gap matches the shape of the bump exactly. Artists such as M. C. Escher used this idea to make tessellations of animals and birds.

items.q: In a geometry app, Isla turns a triangle a half turn about the midpoint of one of its sides. What shape do the triangle and its image make together?
items.e: The half turn puts a copy of the triangle against the same side, upside down. The two triangles make a parallelogram, which has two pairs of parallel sides. Rows of parallelograms tessellate, so any triangle tessellates.

items.q: In a honeycomb pattern of regular hexagons, how many other hexagons share a side with each hexagon (not at the edge)?
items.e: A hexagon has 6 sides, and each side is shared with one neighbour, so it touches 6 others. (3 is the number of hexagons that meet at each corner.)

items.q: A trail of footprints in the sand goes left foot, right foot, left foot, right foot. How is each footprint made from the one before?
items.e: A right foot is a mirror image of a left foot, so there is a reflection. The footprint is also further along the beach, so there is a translation too.

items.q: Ruby turns a square tile a quarter turn about one corner, again and again. How many tiles fit around that corner?
items.e: Each quarter turn is 90°. 360° ÷ 90° = 4, so 4 tiles fill the space around the corner.

items.q: Which tile could NOT be used on its own to cover a floor with no gaps?
items.e: Regular octagons (135°) leave square gaps, which is why octagon floors have small square tiles between them. Rectangles, regular hexagons and equilateral triangles cover a floor on their own.

items.q: In an art project, a pattern has 1 regular hexagon and some equilateral triangles at every corner. How many triangles are at each corner?
items.e: The hexagon’s angle is 120°, so 360° − 120° = 240° is left. 240° ÷ 60° = 4 triangles.

items.q: In a honeycomb pattern, which transformation moves a hexagon onto the next hexagon in the same row?
items.e: All the hexagons face the same way, so each one is the one before slid along: a translation. A quarter turn would not put a hexagon onto its neighbour.

items.q: Chloe is tiling a bathroom floor that is 2 m long and 1.5 m wide with square tiles 50 cm long. How many tiles are needed?
items.e: Change metres to centimetres: 200 cm and 150 cm. 200 ÷ 50 = 4 tiles along and 150 ÷ 50 = 3 tiles across. 4 × 3 = 12 tiles. (4 + 3 = 7 adds instead of multiplying.)

items.q: A kitchen splashback is 120 cm long and 60 cm high. It is covered with square tiles 20 cm long. How many tiles are needed?
items.e: 120 ÷ 20 = 6 tiles along and 60 ÷ 20 = 3 tiles up. 6 × 3 = 18 tiles. (6 is only one row.)

items.q: Tiles for the splashback cost $3.50 each. How much do 18 tiles cost?
A classroom floor is 8 m long and 6 m wide. Carpet tiles are squares 50 cm long. How many carpet tiles cover the floor?
items.e: 50 cm is half a metre, so 2 tiles fit in each metre. 8 m = 16 tiles along and 6 m = 12 tiles across. 16 × 12 = 192 tiles. (48 is the area in square metres, not the number of tiles.)

items.q: A border of tiles 15 cm long runs along a wall 3 m long. How many tiles are in the border?
Floor tiles come in boxes of 12. A tiler needs 100 tiles. How many boxes must be bought?
items.e: 100 ÷ 12 = 8 remainder 4. 8 boxes hold only 96 tiles, so a 9th box is needed for the last 4 tiles.

items.q: Mosaic tiles for a school mural cost $2.40 each. How much do 25 tiles cost?
A tile pattern has a square, a regular hexagon and a regular dodecagon at every corner. The square’s angle is 90° and the hexagon’s angle is 120°. What is the angle of the dodecagon?
items.e: The angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° − 90° − 120° = 150°. (270° and 240° take away only one of the angles; 210° uses 60° for the hexagon.)

items.q: In a geometry app, Ruby reflects the point (2, 3) in the line x = 5, then translates it 2 squares up. Where does it end up?
items.e: (2, 3) is 3 squares left of x = 5, so its image is 3 squares right: (8, 3). Then 2 up: (8, 5).

items.q: Grace designs a logo in a drawing program. The point (7, 4) is rotated a half turn about (5, 4). Where does it go?
items.e: (7, 4) is 2 squares right of (5, 4). A half turn turns right into left, so the image is 2 squares left: (3, 4). (5, 6) and (5, 2) are quarter turns; (1, 4) is too far.

items.q: A stamp makes a pattern along a strip. The first print is at x = 1, and each new print is translated 4 squares right. What is the x-coordinate of the 6th print?
items.e: From the 1st print to the 6th print there are 5 moves: 1 + 5 × 4 = 21. (25 counts 6 moves.)

items.q: Kai wants to tile a floor with regular pentagons only. What will happen?
c: The tiles will fit with no gaps
The tiles will fit if they are made smaller
The tiles will fit if there is an even number
There will be gaps between the tiles
items.e: Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°. 3 × 108° = 324° leaves a 36° gap at every corner. Making the tiles smaller does not change the angles.

items.q: A patio of 3 square metres is paved with hexagon pavers. Each paver covers 0.1 square metres. About how many pavers are needed?
items.e: 3 ÷ 0.1 = 30 pavers (10 pavers cover each square metre, and 3 × 10 = 30).

items.q: A standard Australian brick is 230 mm long. In a brick wall, each row is translated half a brick along. How far is each row moved?
items.e: Half of 230 mm is 230 ÷ 2 = 115 mm.

items.q: A garden path is 4 m long and 2 pavers wide. The pavers are squares 40 cm long. How many pavers are needed?
items.e: 4 m = 400 cm. 400 ÷ 40 = 10 pavers along, and the path is 2 pavers wide: 10 × 2 = 20 pavers.

items.q: In a coding program, a tile is rotated 270° clockwise. Which rotation ends in the same position?
items.e: A full turn is 360°. 270° clockwise is 90° short of a full turn, which is the same as turning 90° the other way, anticlockwise.

items.q: A sprite is translated 3 squares right and 2 squares up, then 1 square left and 4 squares up. Which single translation does the same?
items.e: Across: 3 right and 1 left make 2 right. Up: 2 up and 4 up make 6 up.

items.q: Aarav is making a quilt that is 5 blocks across and 6 blocks down. Each block has 4 triangles in a pinwheel. How many triangles are there?
items.e: 5 × 6 = 30 blocks. 30 × 4 = 120 triangles.

items.q: A mural design has 2 equal regular octagons and a square at each corner. What is the angle of each octagon?
items.e: 360° − 90° = 270° for the two octagons. 270° ÷ 2 = 135° each. (270° forgets to share between the two octagons.)

items.q: Ava says regular octagons tessellate on their own because 8 is an even number. Which reason shows she is wrong?
c: Even numbers of sides never tessellate
Octagons are too big to tile
135° does not divide into 360°: 2 make 270° and 3 make 405°
items.e: What matters is the angle, not the number of sides. Squares (4 sides) and hexagons (6 sides) do tessellate, but octagons leave a 90° gap at every corner.
